articles.title: Adjusted For Inflation, Net Tuition Costs Are Declining At Public Universities
articles.summary: Adjusted for inflation, tuition and fees at public colleges and universities are cheaper now than they were a decade ago. according to the College Board’s la...
articles.body:
Adjusted for inflation, tuition and fees at public colleges and universities are cheaper now than they were a decade ago. according to the College Board's Trends in College Pricing and Student Aid 2026 report released last week.

Between academic years 2016-17 and 2026-27, average inflation-adjusted tuition and fees remained unchanged for students attending private nonprofit colleges and universities, while they declined by 8% for public four-year in-state students, and decreased by 12% for public two-year in-district students. Those are significant turnarounds compared to increases of 20% or more in each of those sectors during the previous two decades.

After adjusting for inflation, 42 states saw declines in their average in-district tuition and fees at public two-year colleges, and 41 states saw declines in their average in-state tuition and fees at public four-year institutions in the last five years.

According to the report, the average published tuition and fees for AY 2026-27 were:

$12,290 for in-state students at public 4-year colleges, up $350, or 2.9%, over the previous year;

$32,730 for out-of-state students at public 4-year colleges, up $1,110, or 3.5%;

$4,210 for in-district students at public two-year colleges, up $100, or 2.4%; and

$46,350 at private nonprofit 4-year colleges, up $1,640, or 3.7%.

These annual increases, shown above, are before adjusting for inflation.

Published "sticker" tuition prices attract the lion's share of press coverage, frequently sensationalized by headlines of tuition costs closing in on or crossing the $100,000 mark, but they convey a false impression about the true costs of college tuition. For that number, we need to consider "net tuition," which is the cost that students actually pay after receiving institutional and other financial aid grants. Those figures write a different narrative. Inflation-adjusted net tuition costs have fallen on average over the past decade:

After adjusting for inflation, the average net tuition and fees paid by first-time, full-time in-state students at public four-year institutions peaked in 2012-13 at $4,600 (in 2026 dollars) and declined to an estimated $1,920 in 2026-27;

The average net tuition and fees (in 2026-27 dollars) paid by first-time full-time students enrolled in private, nonprofit four-year institutions stayed roughly the same at about $20,000 (in 2026 dollars) between 2006-07 and 2019-20 before dropping to an estimated $17,280 in 2026-27.

On average, first-time, full-time, in-district students attending public two- year colleges have received enough grant aid to cover their tuition and fees since academic year 2009-10.

articles.title: Trump’s $1.5 Trillion Defense Budget to Be Blocked by Democrats
articles.summary: Republicans’ midterm defeat is crushing any remaining hopes that Congress would approve President Donald Trump’s unprecedented $1.5 trillion defense budget r...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Republicans' midterm defeat is crushing any remaining hopes that Congress would approve President Donald Trump's unprecedented $1.5 trillion defense budget request amid an unpopular war in the Middle East.

Democrats, who won solid majorities of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, were already largely opposed to the 44% increase from the previous fiscal year and are now signaling they will block any efforts to push it forward.

At the same time, Republican lawmakers returning to the lame-duck session before the new Congress is seated in January may not be able to muster the support or political will to ram through the massive defense spending package, especially amid the Pentagon's unpopular war against Iran that cost many of them their jobs.

"We must push for the development of a more realistic and sustainable approach to our national security — one that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or one paid for with draconian cuts to critical domestic programs," Representative Adam Smith of Washington, the incoming chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, said in a statement after the election.

The Democratic resistance risks imperiling some of Trump's splashiest defense ambitions, including the Golden Dome missile shield and his Trump-class battleship plan, and bodes poorly for defense contractors — some of which also face the prospect of congressional scrutiny over alleged conflicts of interest with the Trump administration.

Shares of major contractors, including Lockheed Martin Corp. and Northrop Grumman Corp., fell this week as the midterm results eroded expectations of a ramp-up in US military spending.

Lawmakers returning to Washington on Monday are going to have to grapple with the annual defense policy bill and a spending plan for fiscal year 2027 — which began on Oct. 1 under stopgap funding that runs out on Dec. 11. Both those measures are now in limbo.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth justified Trump's steep fiscal 2027 budget request by arguing the funds would kickstart badly needed defense modernization efforts as autonomous systems change modern warfare.

But the sheer size of the increase — combined with domestic spending cuts, the growing costs of the Iran war and expensive projects like the Trump-class battleships — grated on lawmakers, including Republicans. And newly emboldened Democrats are likely to be far more motivated to kill off these massive defense spending plans than Republicans are to defend them in the lame-duck session.

articles.title: Facebook recovery scams use fake FBI profiles
articles.summary: Facebook ads promising to recover stolen funds are targeting scam victims again, and Meta confirmed removing flagged accounts after investigation.
articles.body: You've already lost money to a scam. You're frustrated and probably wondering whether you'll ever see that money again. Then, while scrolling through Facebook, an advertisement appears promising to recover your stolen funds. Suddenly, there's a little hope. Maybe someone out there can actually help. Unfortunately, that moment of hope is exactly what scammers are trying to exploit. One of our loyal CyberGuy followers, Patrick K, recently tipped us off to suspicious fraud recovery advertisements and profiles appearing on Facebook. He shared screenshots of what he was seeing and urged us to warn others. His tip caught our attention, so we decided to dig deeper and contacted Meta about the suspicious accounts and advertisements. After reviewing the examples we provided, Meta confirmed to CyberGuy that it removed the flagged accounts and ads for violating its impersonation policies. The screenshots Patrick shared are especially concerning. One promotes stolen-asset recovery services. Another uses FBI-related imagery and claims to help people navigate the Internet Crime Complaint Center, better known as IC3. Together, they show how convincing these offers can appear. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE Facebook recovery ads promise to get your money back The first screenshot Patrick shared shows a Facebook advertisement displayed under the name Adam Molina. The promotional image features a smiling man in a business suit against a purple background. The graphic bears the name "DARKTRACER" and asks whether you've lost assets or funds to scammers. Below that message, the ad promotes services like recovering stolen assets and retrieving hacked cryptocurrency wallets. At the bottom, there's a Facebook Messenger button inviting people to send a message. That's what concerns me. Someone who just lost thousands of dollars could see this advertisement and believe they've finally found a solution. After all, it looks like a company offering specialized assistance. And because it appears as a paid Facebook advertisement, some people may assume the advertiser has been thoroughly vetted. Fake FBI investigator profiles create another trap The second screenshot Patrick sent us is even more troubling. It shows a Facebook page displaying the title "Director of Fraud Investigations" and the name Grace K. The cover image features the White House, the FBI's J. Edgar Hoover Building and cryptocurrency graphics. It also displays references to IC3 and the U.S. Department of Justice. The page description claims to help fraud victims navigate the IC3 reporting process. It even suggests that people who lost more than $4,000 may qualify for federal review. That claim appears on the page, but we found no support for such a dollar threshold in the FBI's published guidance. It's a convincing presentation for someone desperately searching for help. The American flags and official-looking graphics create the impression that a federal agency may be involved. But here's what you need to know. The FBI says IC3 has no official social media presence. It never investigates crimes or recovers stolen money through Facebook Messenger or Telegram. That means any Facebook page claiming to represent IC3 should immediately raise suspicion, regardless of how official it looks. Meta's subsequent removal of the flagged accounts and advertisements reinforces those concerns. Meta removes Facebook recovery scam accounts after CyberGuy inquiry After CyberGuy shared Patrick's screenshots with Meta, the company investigated and confirmed that it removed the flagged accounts and advertisements for violating its impersonation policies. Meta also provided broader details about its efforts to combat these schemes. According to the company, it removed more than 179 million accounts, Pages and Groups for misrepresenting identity during the first half of 2026. Most were removed before anyone reported them. Since 2025, Meta says it has also removed more than 17.3 million Facebook and Instagram accounts linked to criminal scam centers. This problem isn't new to Meta. The company previously worked with cybersecurity researchers at Graphika to identify fraudulent websites impersonating the FBI's IC3 complaint center. The scammers promised to help victims recover stolen money, including cryptocurrency. Meta says it blocked the fraudulent websites and removed accounts connected to those operations. However, the examples Patrick discovered show how these impersonation schemes continue to reach Facebook users. FBI warns about fake IC3 recovery investigators On July 20, 2026, the FBI issued an updated public warning about scammers impersonating IC3 investigators. According to the agency, criminals create fraudulent social media profiles that appear connected to the FBI. They then approach people who have already reported losing money to online scams. In one documented scheme, a victim realizes they've been defrauded and threatens to report the crime to the FBI. Later, someone pretending to be an FBI agent contacts the victim through Facebook Messenger. The conversation may move to Telegram, where the impersonator provides a link supposedly connected to the victim's IC3 complaint. That link may contain malicious code or collect additional financial information. Either way, the victim faces another potential loss. The FBI also warns about AI-generated videos impersonating federal officials. Some of these videos direct victims to fraudulent websites designed to resemble the real IC3 complaint center. Once there, visitors may be asked to submit personal information under the impression they're dealing with federal investigators. And this type of impersonation extends well beyond Facebook. In a separate September 17, 2026, warning, the FBI reported nearly 61,000 complaints involving law enforcement or government impersonation scams between January 2025 and July 2026. Reported losses exceeded $1.6 billion. Those figures cover a broad range of government impersonation schemes, not Facebook recovery scams specifically. However, they show how costly impersonating official authorities has become. SCAMMERS ARE COMING FOR YOUR MONEY. HERE’S THE ONE THING YOU MUST NEVER DO Why scammers target people who already lost money There's a particularly cruel element to recovery fraud. The criminals approach people who may already be dealing with serious financial hardship. Some have lost retirement savings, while others have been tricked into sending cryptocurrency to someone they trusted. When an offer arrives promising to recover those funds, it's understandable why someone might want to believe it. In August 2026, the Federal Trade Commission warned that recovery scammers sometimes purchase lists of people who previously lost money to fraud. They use those details to make their offers appear credible. For example, someone may contact you claiming they've located your stolen funds. They might even know approximately how much you lost. That information can make the person sound legitimate, especially when they claim to represent a government agency or law firm. Eventually, the supposed recovery agent introduces a fee. They might call it a processing charge or claim the payment will release your recovered funds. But after you pay, the promised refund never arrives. In some cases, the scammer also collects enough personal information to attempt identity theft. We've previously covered the scripts criminals use in cryptocurrency scams, including fake recovery services that demand additional cryptocurrency payments. How to spot Facebook recovery scams before losing more money A convincing advertisement or official-looking Facebook profile can fool someone who's searching for answers. Fortunately, there are warning signs you can look for before responding. Here's how to protect yourself. 1. Be suspicious of guaranteed recovery promises Anyone claiming they can definitely retrieve stolen cryptocurrency or recover all your lost money deserves close scrutiny. Recovery depends on the circumstances, and no legitimate service can guarantee success. Be especially cautious when someone promises fast results. 2. Never pay an unexpected upfront recovery fee The FTC warns that scammers often demand processing fees before supposedly releasing recovered funds. These payments may be described as taxes or administrative charges. However, the FBI says IC3 never charges victims to recover stolen money. 3. Check claims of government involvement If someone on Facebook claims to work for IC3, don't engage. The FBI says IC3 has no official social media presence. Instead, type IC3.gov directly into your browser to verify information or submit a complaint. 4. Watch for conversations moving to other apps Scammers may begin contacting you through Facebook Messenger before asking to continue on Telegram. The FBI specifically identified this behavior in IC3 impersonation cases. Be cautious when an unexpected contact pressures you to switch platforms. 5. Protect your financial information Never share banking passwords or cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases with someone advertising recovery services. Also, don't install remote-access software at the request of an unexpected contact. Doing so could give scammers access to your accounts or device. 6. Research recovery companies independently Search for the company's name alongside terms such as "scam" or "complaint." Look for independently verifiable business information and a legitimate track record. Keep in mind that scammers can create fake testimonials and misleading websites to appear trustworthy. Use strong antivirus software Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious websites, phishing links and harmful downloads associated with recovery scams. However, antivirus software cannot prevent every scam, especially if you're tricked into sending money yourself. Report suspicious Facebook advertisements Select the three-dot menu in the upper-right corner of the advertisement and choose Report ad. Then follow the prompts. These details may help Facebook and law enforcement investigate the activity. What to do if you already contacted a recovery scammer If you've exchanged messages with someone offering to recover stolen money, stop communicating until you've independently verified who you're dealing with. And if you've already sent money, act quickly. Here's what to do next. Remember, legitimate recovery options may exist through financial institutions or law enforcement investigations. Always contact these organizations directly using their official websites or verified phone numbers rather than information provided by someone who approached you online. Kurt's key takeaways I have to give Patrick credit for bringing these suspicious Facebook ads to our attention. After we followed up with Meta, the company investigated and removed the accounts and ads we flagged. That's a positive outcome, and I appreciate Meta taking action. Still, the bigger problem remains. Scammers continue targeting people who have already lost money, often using convincing government branding to gain their trust. articles.title: Democrats plot to choke off Iran war — with some GOP help
articles.summary: Democrats, on the wings of the big midterm wave, are looking to grind President Trump’s war with Iran to a halt once they retake the majority next year. Senate Democrats say they have some Republican support to end the conflict, which has dragged on for more than eight months, and have threatened to use the…
articles.body:
Democrats, on the wings of the big midterm wave , are looking to grind President Trump’s war with Iran to a halt once they retake the majority next year.

Senate Democrats say they have some Republican support to end the conflict, which has dragged on for more than eight months, and have threatened to use the “power of the purse” to deprive the Pentagon of funds needed to wage the war.

Both Trump and Vice President Vance pointed to the Iran war as the main culprit for why Republicans experienced an electoral wipeout, with Democrats taking the majority in the House, Senate, governors’ mansions and statehouses.

“We are going to end the war. We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said at a press conference Wednesday.

Four Republican senators — Thom Tillis (N.C.), Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), and Rand Paul (Ky.) — previously backed Democrats on a resolution to direct the commander in chief to withdraw U.S. service members from hostilities against Iran, barring formal congressional authorization for use of military force.

Congress is staring down a Dec. 11 timeline to fund the government or suffer a shutdown, less than a month before the majorities in both chambers switch. It’s unclear whether Republicans will attempt to pass one final reconciliation bill before losing control, which could include emergency Iran war funding.

Candidates on both sides of the aisle criticized the Iran war during their campaigns, as it became less and less popular. The conflict has cost at least $47 billion , while causing energy prices to skyrocket. Trump had long promised to keep the U.S. out of foreign wars.

Some Democrats, including at least one with 2028 aspirations , said the House caucus should demand an end to Iran war funding as part of any agreement to keep the government funded, even temporarily.

“Support a continuing resolution prohibiting the financing of any combat activities of the U.S. military in Iran. End the Iran war like we did for Vietnam,” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, wrote on social media Wednesday.

Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), a senior member on the House Appropriations Committee, wrote on social media Friday that “we can’t wait until the next Congress to end the war with Iran – it must end NOW!”

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said this week he will introduce a joint resolution to end Iran on the first day of the next Congress.

“And Democrats will use hearings, legislation, oversight and the power of the purse to push the administration toward a durable, diplomatic solution,” Meeks said in a statement to The Hill. “We will keep fighting to end Trump’s failed war of choice, as we focus on addressing the needs of the American people.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is slated to become House Speaker in January, said in a “Dear Colleague” letter that one the caucus’s priorities will be to stop the “ reckless war of choice ” in Iran.

The White House in June requested $87.6 billion in supplemental funding, which includes $67 billion in Pentagon funding. The package has not gone far in Congress with increased Democratic opposition.

The typically bipartisan National Defense Authorization Act is on shaky ground this year amid partisan infighting. Democrats think the policy bill’s top-line number should be shaved off hundreds of billions of dollars, and they are demanding guardrails around the U.S. war with Iran.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Saturday during Crooked Media’s “Crooked Con” event in Washington, D.C., that Democrats should halt funding for White House operations to make the president end the conflict.

“We control that. So if he can’t find a way out of this, we can put pressure on him,” Kelly said in reference to Trump. Hours later, Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), who is on the Senate Intelligence Committee, endorsed Kelly’s pitch .

Rep. Nikki Budzinski (D-Ill.), who is expected to be the next chair of the New Democrat Coalition, said the Democrats’ leverage to end the Iran war rests in the funding process. But she also wants answers from the Pentagon about what victory looks like.

“I do think that it’s through the Defense budget and the appropriations process. It is the power of the purse. I think we know that this administration put out a ridiculous, eye-popping amount to Congress to fund this war. There’s going to be no appetite for that. And so, I think that that is going to be, probably, the most important tool that we’re going to have in our toolbox to hold them accountable,” Budzinski said in a phone interview with The Hill.

“But I also am eager, beyond just the appropriations process, to have them come before Congress to explain what does success — they still have not articulated what success looks like,” the Illinois Democrat said.

Some top House Republicans agree about the lack of strategy over the war, which has emptied out the U.S. military magazines of top-tier weapons systems and left U.S. bases in the Middle East severely damaged by Iranian attacks.

Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), who chairs the powerful House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, declined on Friday to say whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should be impeached or otherwise removed from office.

“But I can tell you with a high level of confidence that … there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth,” Comer said Friday during his appearance on NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner.

“We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran, and I think the Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters,” Comer said.

House Democrats, who have long called for Hegseth’s removal , said the oversight will not stop there. They are also encouraging their GOP colleagues to pass a bill that would prohibit the use of additional funds for the war without congressional approval.

“And every Republican who suddenly found the courage to oppose the war come election season better put their money where their mouth is and vote to end the war and pass my bill to prevent Trump from spending a single dollar more on it,” Rep. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.), another House Armed Services Committee member and former Army intelligence officer, said in a statement to The Hill.

articles.title: Ex-RFK Jr adviser requests records on Wiles’s health policy influence
articles.summary: Calley Means, a former top adviser to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., requested records on former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’s health policy influence be preserved following allegations he made that she led the Trump administration to consistently bow to corporate interests on health policy. “In light of…
articles.body:
Calley Means, a former top adviser to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., requested records on former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’s health policy influence be preserved following allegations he made that she led the Trump administration to consistently bow to corporate interests on health policy.

“In light of suggestions that Susie Wiles and James Blair may pursue legal action over my Joe Rogan interview, I am publicly requesting that she, Ballard Partners, Continental Strategy, and other relevant parties immediately preserve all potentially relevant records and communications,” he wrote on social media Sunday.

Means began his lengthy list asking for Wiles’s communications regarding the sugar industry’s impact on federal nutrition as well as her discussions with GOP pollster Tony Fabrizio, food industry representatives and White House officials about “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) initiatives, school nutrition standards and the proposed federal definition of ultra-processed foods.

He also listed drafts, internal correspondence, meeting notes and communications involving health officials, such as Kennedy, Walker Barrett and Heidi Overton.

The former health adviser concluded his list by requesting records from Continental Strategy — the lobbying firm Wiles’s daughter works for — be preserved.

Means, a Kennedy ally who helped build the MAHA movement, resigned from the administration two weeks ago after clashing with the White House and becoming frustrated over the lack of progress on key MAHA priorities.

He made headlines recently for accusing Wiles of ensuring special interests were making donations to the administration and the GOP to have a monetary advantage in the midterm elections.

Means claimed in an interview with podcaster Joe Rogan that Wiles once told him directly, “I need the money from the sugar people to win the midterms.”

During her tenure as a lobbyist before joining the Trump administration, Means says Wiles took money from the highest-paying clients, including from the pharmaceutical and pesticide industries, as well as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

In another interview with CBS News on Sunday, Means said he believed staffers around President Trump were giving him “severe poor advice” and treating the president “like a baby.”

articles.title: The market bloodbath just exposed Wall Street’s true fears about U.S. debt, top economist warns
articles.summary: "They’re up because of mounting fiscal stress, not because of AI."
articles.body:
There have been competing theories to explain why Treasury yields have risen so much this year, but last week's brutal stock selloff debunked one of them, according to a top economist.

The 10-year yield has eased in recent weeks as investors seek shelter in Treasuries. But before the latest dip, it shot up more 100 basis points, soaring above 5% and at one point hitting the highest level in 24 years.

The run-up began after the Iran war started in late February, sending oil prices up and raising expectations that the Federal Reserve will hike rates to fight suddenly resurgent inflation.

At the same time, hyperscalers have been flooding the bond market with fresh debt to finance massive capital spending and the AI infrastructure boom, which has kept the U.S. economy running hot and inflation sticky.

That's competed for investors' dollars as the Treasury Department taps the bond market to finance the federal government's $2 trillion budget deficit—and pay interest of the $40 trillion in U.S. debt.

Some on Wall Street have downplayed the spike in yields, saying the deluge of AI debt has crowded out U.S. bonds and forced the Treasury to offer investors higher returns at auctions.

But Robin Brooks, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, doesn't buy that explanation. In a Substack post on Saturday , he said the past week's market selloff represented a "natural experiment" that puts the competing arguments to the test.

"On one end of the spectrum are people like me who think this is a rising fiscal risk premium as our public debt grows out of control," he wrote. "On the other end are folks who say it's hyperscaler debt issuance that's pushing up yields, so there's no sign fiscal policy's in trouble."

Brooks said corporate borrowing is nowhere near where it was in the IT bubble of the early 2000s, while public borrowing is historically high and more likely driving up yields.

He pointed to the bond market's reaction to the latest monthly jobs report, which showed payrolls grew by more than double the consensus estimate.

Compared to previous upside job surprises, the two-year yield rose more than what hot economic growth could explain, undercutting the idea that U.S. growth depends on AI as well as the argument that AI is responsible for higher yields.

Brooks also cited the market-implied yield for a 10-year security 10 years from now, which gauges the premium investors demand for the risk of holding Treasuries long term. Such risks include the trajectory of U.S. debt and deficits.

articles.title: Nvidia investigates reports of CEO’s relationship with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board of directors announced it would be opening an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, following reports alleging he had an intimate relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for China. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has…
articles.body:
Nvidia’s board of directors announced it would be opening an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, following reports alleging he had an intimate relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for China.

“The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the board wrote in a statement . “A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.”

The board continued that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets” were compromised by Huang’s relationship with accused Chinese spy and Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

“The Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” it concluded. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

The accusations stemmed from a Thursday New York Times report that claimed American spy agencies last year discovered Alice Huang illegally smuggled advanced AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with Jensen Huang.

While Nvidia and Huang denied the initial report, the CEO reportedly acknowledged on Sunday that he was “unfaithful” to his wife.

“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote, according to a Sunday report from Bloomberg , citing a memo released to the company.

Another report from the Times also found Secretary of State Marco Rubio allegedly oversaw the drafting of the 2025 memo that was sent out regarding Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship, citing multiple people briefed on the matter.

The Nvidia CEO has already been called to appear this month by a group of GOP lawmakers who chair the House Select Committee on China, House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.

They requested Huang appear in a joint, closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 to address concerns regarding Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with … Alice Huang.”

articles.title: Bloodshed in Kolkata flat: How a heated argument turned fatal for 25-year-old techie Sarthak Sarkar; girlfriend, her mother arrested
articles.summary: KOLKATA: A woman ran out of a rented flat in Kolkata in the early hours of Sunday, crying for help.
articles.body: KOLKATA: A woman ran out of a rented flat in Kolkata in the early hours of Sunday, crying for help. Inside, neighbours found her 25-year-old live-in partner lying in a pool of blood on the bed.The man had allegedly been attacked with a sharp weapon following a heated argument, with his partner and her mother now arrested in connection with his death. The incident took place at Fartabad in Garia late on Saturday night.Who was the victim?The deceased, Sarthak Sarkar, was a resident of Barasat and worked as a software engineer at a company in Salt Lake's Sector V.He had been living in a rented flat in Fartabad with his girlfriend and live-in partner, Sanchalika. Her mother, Moumita, also stayed with the couple.What happened inside the flat?According to preliminary police investigations, an argument broke out between Sarthak and Sanchalika over an issue on Saturday night.During the altercation, Sanchalika allegedly attacked him with a sharp weapon, striking him on the shoulder. Sarthak was rushed to hospital, where doctors declared him dead.Police suspect that Sanchalika's mother may also have played a role in the incident. Investigators are trying to establish what led to the argument and whether Moumita was involved in the alleged attack.Neighbours heard arguments before midnightThe incident came to light around 1.30 am, when a woman reportedly ran out of the flat, crying and seeking help.Residents rushed to the spot and found the young man lying in a pool of blood on the bed. The woman who had sought help had several scratch marks on her neck.“We were still awake when we heard a woman crying and asking for help. articles.title: China Extends Pause on 24% US Tariffs to January, Keeps 10% Rate
articles.summary: China will suspend an additional 24% tariff on US goods for another two months, formalizing a decision by the two countries’ leaders to prolong their trade t...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- China will suspend an additional 24% tariff on US goods for another two months, formalizing a decision by the two countries' leaders to prolong their trade truce until next January.

The move will take effect at 1:01 p.m. Beijing time on Tuesday, with a 10% blanket tariff retained on US imports, the Customs Tariff Commission of the State Council said in a statement. China will also extend its suspension of special fees on American ships docking at its ports until Jan. 10, the Transport Ministry said in a separate statement on Monday.

The new timeline is a result of the agreement reached by Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in September to extend their tariff ceasefire until early next year. The truce, originally set to expire on Nov. 10, was struck in Busan, South Korea in October 2025, where both sides agreed to suspend their mutual 24% levies while leaving the 10% rate in place.

The US and China imposed the levies at the start of their tit-for-tat trade escalation started by Trump shortly after he returned to the White House last year.

China said it will closely monitor US plans to replace Trump's emergency tariffs — which were overturned by the Supreme Court earlier this year — with duties imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. In the statement, it warned that Beijing may adjust its countermeasures accordingly.

Trump and Xi are set to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen later this month for what will be their third summit this year. At their last round of talks in Washington in September, they agreed to extend the trade truce until Jan. 10.

While US-China ties have stabilized, signs of tensions have lingered.

Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer spoke with China's Vice Premier He Lifeng, raising concerns about Beijing's recent actions and the importance of implementing commitments made as part of the deal reached in Busan.

In a statement, Greer's office said he used a video call to emphasize the critical importance for China to take "concrete actions" to implement its pledges, specifically on "agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals."

articles.title: Meet the 5 Democrats poised to shake up Washington’s AI safety debate
articles.summary: The AI safety community is feeling optimistic after the Democrats’ midterm sweep elected several candidates promising stricter regulations on the technology. After years of stalled AI regulation in Congress, advocates for stricter guardrails on the technology are hopeful the new class of House and Senate members could turn the tide in their favor. While AI…
articles.body:
The AI safety community is feeling optimistic after the Democrats’ midterm sweep elected several candidates promising stricter regulations on the technology.

After years of stalled AI regulation in Congress, advocates for stricter guardrails on the technology are hopeful the new class of House and Senate members could turn the tide in their favor.

While AI was not the top issue for voters, it played a significant role, with candidates across the country floating proposals to quell concerns over technology safety, job security and data centers.

Now, several of these candidates are heading to Washington, offering a “reset” on AI policy, advocates told The Hill.

“It’s an opportunity for people on both sides of the aisle to reconsider how they want to approach this topic of AI. There is now this feeling of great possibility,” Connor Leahy, an AI researcher leading the nonprofit Control AI, which argues for ending development of superintelligence.

Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI safety, said it’s “an incredibly hopeful outcome for humanity.”

Here’s who to watch on AI safety in Congress next year.

California state Sen. Scott Wiener (D), who will fill the seat of former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), was one of the first state lawmakers to push legislation to address AI safety concerns.

Wiener was the lead author behind California’s S.B. 1047, the Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act, one of the first policy proposals to require AI models to undergo safety testing before public release.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) eventually vetoed the legislation, but a later bill authored by Wiener, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, or S.B. 53, was signed by the governor last year.

S.B. 53 established new transparency requirements for large AI labs, including mandated safety frameworks along with transparency and safety incident reporting. New York and Illinois later passed similar bills.

On the campaign trail, Wiener said he would craft legislation on AI “kill switches,” safety standards, legal liability and international partnerships. He also vowed to expand unemployment benefits ahead of potential job displacement and use tax policy to ensure AI’s benefits are distributed to the public

“Congress hasn’t acted. I did. I took on Big Tech,” Wiener said in one ad.

He will represent most of San Francisco, where many of the most popular AI tools are developed.

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel (D-Colo.), who unseated Republican Gabe Evans in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, was one of the AI safety community’s most-anticipated candidates. He received monetary support from several political action committees on AI safety, including Public First and one run by crypto billionaire Chris Larsen.

Rutinel sponsored various AI safety laws in Colorado, including a first-in-the-nation law requiring “high-risk” AI developers to “use reasonable care to avoid algorithmic discrimination.” He has also spoken out about the existential risks around the technology.

Shortly before the bill was supposed to go into effect, Colorado repealed it and replaced it with a narrower measure.

Rutinel leaned into the populist sentiment among voters, arguing the AI firms “are putting profits ahead of people.” He has also advocated for protections for AI whistleblowers, mandatory incident reporting and independent testing of AI systems.

Like Rutinel, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) takes a populist approach to the technology and the companies developing it.

In an in-depth AI policy platform released last June, El-Sayed became the first politician to call for public ownership of frontier AI firms, going a step further than his ally, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

The Vermont independent last month proposed far-reaching measures to control AI development, including a sovereign wealth fund that would take 50 percent stakes in the country’s largest companies and use them to give Americans an annual paycheck.

“AI isn’t just any other tool. Even today, it holds the capacity to destroy our jobs, deny our healthcare and surveil us,” El-Sayed said on the campaign trail. “That power can’t sit solely within the control of a few billionaires.”

The Michigan progressive, meanwhile, proposes requiring all frontier AI labs to be chartered as public benefit corporations to ensure “profit cannot come at the cost of public safety, civil rights or democratic integrity.”

His proposal includes an automation levy, or a pre-worker-equivalent tax on AI-driven automation, that can be used for education, unemployment benefits, wage insurance and small business revolving loans.

El-Sayed has also discussed AI safety, calling for a federal agency like the Food and Drug Administration to test models before they are deployed.

A similar idea was floated at one point by officials in the Trump administration, though President Trump instead created a voluntary testing framework for AI labs.

McCoy said he is “incredibly excited” for El-Sayed’s role in the upper chamber.

El-Sayed “made clear that this is a top issue for him, recognizing the ways AI is putting our economy, our jobs, and our safety at risk, and is bringing his fierce intelligence and relentless dedication to bear on the problem,” McCoy added.

Rep.-elect Micah Lasher (D-N.Y.) is heading to Washington to represent New York’s 12th Congressional District. The primary race for the Democratic nomination was one of the most closely watched races for the tech industry, but not because of Lasher.

Lasher beat out New York State Assembly member Alex Bores, who had more than $8 million spent against him by the Silicon Valley-backed super PAC Leading the Future. The opposition campaign put Bores’s name on the radar, prompting more than $20 billion in support from AI safety groups.

Bores was targeted because of his campaign on AI safety concerns and sponsorship of New York’s Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act. Like California’s S.B. 53, the law requires AI firms to publish information about their safety protocols.

While Bores lost, Lasher is also a vocal critic of unregulated AI. Lasher was a co-sponsor of the RAISE Act. According to his campaign website , Lasher introduced a bill to create a first-in-the-nation insurance program in New York state.

He also co-sponsored legislation to impose a moratorium on new data center projects in New York, along with proposals to safeguard the use of AI in hiring decisions and in the classroom.

Rep.-elect Sam Forstag (Mont.) was one of several Democrats across the country to flip a GOP seat. Forstag, a former smokejumper and union leader, will represent Montana’s 1st District, covering the city of Missoula and the western portion of the state.

Forstag beat out Aaron Flint, who received more than $500,000 from American Mission PAC, affiliated with the Leading the Future network.

“Sam Forstag took on the chosen candidate of the anti-regulation super PAC and won, running on a strong platform that would rein in data centers, put guardrails on AI development, and stand up for workers, kids, and businesses harmed by AI,” McCoy told The Hill.

Leading the Future pushed back on claims it is against regulation, maintaining it supports candidates who will help advance a “positive, forward-looking agenda for AI innovation” in Washington.

Like others on this list, Forstag expressed concerns about AI’s existential risks, especially after an ominous warning from an AI researcher about the advancing capabilities of self-improving AI.

Congress has “not done a damn thing to provide any sort of safety precautions for these AI companies,” Forstag said in a video in September, adding, “this technology is moving incredibly quickly and Congress is moving too damn slow.”

articles.title: Musk spent big on Republicans in the midterms. He has little to show for it
articles.summary: Elon Musk poured millions of dollars into boosting Republicans in the midterm elections, but the tech mogul’s vast wealth was no match for the blue wave that battered the GOP on Tuesday night. Despite spending more than $442 million this cycle — a massive sum that eclipsed his support for President Trump in the 2024 election — Republicans…
articles.body:
Elon Musk poured millions of dollars into boosting Republicans in the midterm elections, but the tech mogul’s vast wealth was no match for the blue wave that battered the GOP on Tuesday night.

Despite spending more than $442 million this cycle — a massive sum that eclipsed his support for President Trump in the 2024 election — Republicans lost ground across the country, even in territory considered relatively safe for the party.

The GOP’s drubbing underscored the limits of the world’s richest man in shaping the political map and raises questions about how his business empire will fare under Democratic leaders in his home base of Texas and on Capitol Hill.

“Other than the Republicans, Elon Musk is probably the biggest loser of last Tuesday,” said Cayce Myers, a Virginia Tech public relations professor who has focused on political campaigns.

Musk pumped hundreds of millions of dollars into the 2024 presidential race and became a major figure in Trump’s second term, even leading the cost-saving crackdown that led to sweeping cuts and layoffs in the federal government. But after pouring millions into a Wisconsin race that didn’t pay off last year, Musk said he’d scale back political spending .

That pledge didn’t hold for long, and Musk started midterm spending in late 2025 . By Election Day, he was the top donor by a mile.

“You have to have money to be competitive. No question,” Myers added. “But money cannot guarantee outcome.”

Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican strategist and CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI, said “all of the money in the world cannot move voters when they have their minds made up.” He also suggested the impact of Musk’s spending in getting voters to turn out for Trump in 2024 was “overstated,” noting that “money has diminishing returns in politics.”

The billionaire’s political losses Tuesday were starkest in his home state of Texas, where Musk spent at least $168 million boosting embattled Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

Paxton fell to Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race — and Democrats flipped more than a half dozen other statewide roles, including the governor’s office and the attorney general post, turning the state’s top roles blue for the first time in decades.

The Texas Senate became the most expensive nonpresidential race on record, according to AdImpact data just before Election Day, with nearly $575 million spent on the Paxton-Talarico fight. In the general election stretch, pro-Paxton donors spent more than double the money that was spent by the pro-Talarico camp, with a major boost from Musk.

Musk also gave $5 million to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R) reelection bid, according to campaign finance records, only for Abbott to lose to Democrat Gina Hinojosa — a state lawmaker who pledged to put a pause on data center expansion and won a court order last week seeking access to emails between Abbott’s office and Musk.

Meanwhile, Paxton will be replaced as the state’s top prosecutor by Democrat Nathan Johnson, who promised on the campaign trail to investigate grants to Musk’s Starlink and SpaceX.

Democrats also broke into the GOP’s trifecta control over the Texas state Legislature, flipping the House .

“He could have spent $0 and probably seen the same result,” Steinhauser said. “This was a national wave election of historic proportions.”

“Nobody was really prepared for it to be this big,” he continued. “He could have spent $0. He could have spent $450 million in Texas and across the country, and it probably wouldn’t have moved the needle very much.”

The unexpected changing of the guard throughout Texas raises new questions about Musk’s standing. Musk fled from California to Texas to escape left-wing politics and regulators .

“For Elon, the math ain’t mathing,” said Jon Taylor, a political science professor at the University of Texas at San Antonio. “All this to try to keep Texas red, but did he spend it essentially for nothing?”

“The thing that Musk, I think, needs to be worried about is that regulatory structure of the state of Texas is about to change, with an attorney general who’s going to be aggressive against the Trump administration and against Elon Musk,” Taylor said.

Musk himself seemed to read the results that way. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” Musk wrote on the social platform X , which he owns.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he said in another post, seemingly referencing SpaceX’s recent push to develop orbital data centers.

Musk and his companies are also expected to be targets beyond Texas as Democrats take control on Capitol Hill.

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) suggested on X last week that he’d investigate Musk’s links to Russian President Vladimir Putin, after Putin touted the tech mogul as a “real genius.”

Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) posted that Musk “ must answer ” for the cuts and firings undergone by the Department of Government Efficiency. Others have signaled they’ll probe his companies’ multibillion-dollar government contracts .

Stocks in Tesla and SpaceX fell by hundreds of billions of dollars in combined market value in the two days after the midterms amid investor concerns about new hurdles for the billionaire’s companies under Democratic leadership, CNBC reported.

But Steinhauser was skeptical about how hard Democrats will go after Musk himself.

“I think the Democrats will be careful about overreach,” he said. “There will be some questions about investigations and things like that … but I don’t think they’re planning to just go after him personally in the way that maybe some might expect.”

Texas-based Republican consultant Vinny Minchillo argued that “the business of Texas is business,” regardless of the party in power.

“On one hand, listen, he spent a lot of money to support the Republicans, but on the other hand he’s got a gigantic plant in Austin that employs a lot of people, puts a lot of money into the economy, and the SpaceX project does the same,” Minchillo said of Musk.

“There was talk here that: Are the Democrats going to go after Elon Musk somehow? I’m hoping they’re smarter than that.”

Democrats might take aim at Musk and other billionaires’ ability to spend so much on elections.

Talarico, for one, has accused Musk of trying to “buy his own personal U.S. senator” and called after the election for campaign finance reform.

“Somebody should not be able to spend that much money in politics, and I hope that we see reform that prevents that from happening,” said Luke Warford, a founding partner at the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund.

At the same time, Warford forecast that Musk’s business empire will remain a major player in the Lone Star State as the new crop of Democrats takes power.

“Elon is a person who brings a lot of innovation to the state,” he said, “and so I think it’s going to be really interesting to see how it plays out.”

articles.title: Trump: Nvidia CEO an ‘honorable guy’
articles.summary: President Trump called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang an “honorable guy” after reports surfaced that the tech leader had an intimate relationship with accused Chinese spy Alice Huang. Trump told reporters he had not spoken to Jensen Huang — a close ally — about the accusations. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never…
articles.body:
President Trump called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang an “honorable guy” after reports surfaced that the tech leader had an intimate relationship with accused Chinese spy Alice Huang.

Trump told reporters he had not spoken to Jensen Huang — a close ally — about the accusations.

“I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure. I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job, and so I would certainly hope he’s a fine person, in my opinion,” he said.

The allegations stemmed from reporting in The New York Times about a 2025 report from the U.S. intelligence community that alleged Alice Huang illegally smuggled advanced AI chips into China last year while developing a “close relationship” with the tech mogul.

Asked if Trump wished he had acted on this intelligence sooner: “I think, you know, I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse … he’s done an amazing job for our country.”

Jensen Huang previously accompanied the president on a trip to Beijing, and his company, Nvidia, remains one of the only U.S. companies allowed to sell certain AI chips to China.

Trump is slated to travel to Asia next week, though he said he doesn’t know if the billionaire will come with him this time.

“I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him,” he expressed. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong. He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.”

The CEO reportedly acknowledged on Sunday that he was “unfaithful” to his wife in a message to the company after an Nvidia spokesperson initially dismissed the report concerning the relationship.

“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote, according to a Sunday report from Bloomberg , citing a memo released to the company.

Trump’s staunch backing of Huang comes after Nvidia announced it would be opening an “ independent investigation ” into its CEO on Sunday regarding the allegations. A similar probe from top GOP lawmakers was also launched, with the lawmakers calling Huang to appear on Nov. 18 for a joint, closed-door briefing.

articles.title: Jonathan Kanter is using AI to take on Big Tech
articles.summary: Former Biden-era Justice Department Antitrust Division chief Jonathan Kanter built an AI legal tech tool with ex-government colleagues to take on big corporations.
articles.body: When Jonathan Kanter stepped down as head of the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division in 2024, he set out to keep fighting to dismantle illegal monopolies. But this time, he’s continuing the fight in the private sector, and with a perhaps unexpected tool: AI. Alongside former acting Antitrust Division chief Doha Mekki, Kanter recently launched a new tech startup, FluxCap. The team is stacked with former DOJ staffers and former Palantir engineers, and it’s selling an AI-based legal research and analysis tool that helps plaintiffs build and strengthen cases against the kinds of well-heeled companies Kanter and Mekki took on at the Antitrust Division. FluxCap is launching with a focus on antitrust cases, but it plans to expand into other practice areas as well. Kanter imagines FluxCap as a “force multiplier” for antitrust watchdogs taking on powerful opponents in Big Tech and elsewhere. “This, to me, it’s existential,” he tells The Verge in an interview. “Because it’s the only way that enforcement is going to work in the long term, is if technology and other tools are able to help scarce resources go significantly further than they can today.” FluxCap’s platform, built off proprietary technology and existing large language models, is primarily intended for research and analysis. It’s trained to pick up the facts and legal framework that will determine whether a case succeeds, then find potential holes in attorneys’ logic. To help attorneys prepare for trial, FluxCap can also help sift through vast piles of discovery materials, searching for signals that a company acted in anticompetitive ways. It’s part of a wave of legal tech tools that are using AI to try to help lawyers do more with less and make the legal process more efficient. Getting the tool to find relevant evidence was one of the hardest parts, Kanter says. Executives are unlikely to come out and say they’re monopolists, but surrounding context can give a very specific meaning to certain messages. In the antitrust trial against Live Nation-Ticketmaster, for example, the government played a recorded phone call between the Live Nation CEO and a customer who decided to switch to a different ticketing platform. In response, the CEO reminded the customer that a new arena in town could make it harder to deliver as many concerts to his venue. The customer testified he took it as a “not-so-veiled” threat that Live Nation could cut off events programming if he didn’t also accept its ticketing service. FluxCap’s team of former government lawyers spent months testing the system with existing and hypothetical test cases to see if it could really help build a solid argument. Getting “basic legal tools” (which Kanter calls “BLTs”) to understand that kind of nuance is difficult because “lawyering isn’t about right or wrong answers,” he says. “Both sides can be right and both sides can be wrong. And what you’re essentially trying to do is you’re trying to persuade a court, a jury, a regulator to reach a certain outcome.” The team counts antitrust boutique firm Kressin Powers as one of its first customers, and Kanter says it’s in talks with both public and private enforcers. “It gives them that virtual capacity so that a small team can take on a large team,” Kanter says, adding that it provides the manpower of roughly “20-plus people working around the clock.” The seeds of FluxCap began inside the Antitrust Division, where Kanter and his team were already trying to stretch their limited resources with technology. During the Biden administration, the DOJ went to trial against Google twice and brought monopolization suits against Apple and Live Nation, among other actions. But the Division’s resources and staff pale in comparison to companies with multibillion- to trillion-dollar market caps and large legal teams to review documents and mount defenses. The entire Antitrust Division was appropriated $245 million by Congress for fiscal year 2026, with more than 400 attorneys on staff across several issue areas. The imbalance is even greater for state attorneys general, who have pushed forward with antitrust action as the Trump administration has hung back. Earlier this year, state AGs won a case against Live Nation that the DOJ under the Trump administration settled, and states also sued to block the Paramount-Warner Media merger before ultimately settling, when the DOJ declined. “A large state AG might have 10 people working on a case,” Kanter says. “It’s just not realistic to have the resources necessary to take on these big companies.” During Kanter’s time as antitrust head, he and others tried AI-based BLTs but found them lacking for complex legal research. “Every antitrust lawyer has tried asking questions to ChatGPT or [AI legal research software] Harvey or one of those tools, and they do okay,” Kanter says. “But they miss the nuance.” While Kanter was at the DOJ, the Antitrust Division secured a $45.5 million grant from the government’s Tech Modernization Fund to implement better tools for managing cases and reviewing evidence. Kanter says his team “never had the opportunity to put that to work” before leaving office, but what they’re building now is “even more ambitious and better than I could have imagined when I was at DOJ.” Tech alone can’t fully even the playing field, Kanter says. “Government is always going to be outmatched, and they desperately need more funding, and desperately need more budget, and more headcount.” Even if that happens, however, private defendants are likely to “far outweigh anything that the government could ever produce, whether it’s federal government or states or private plaintiffs,” he says. “We believe this will be the great equalizer that will allow those teams to go toe to toe with anyone regardless of their size and regardless how deep their pockets are.”

articles.title: Medium is launching a new note-taking app called TK
articles.summary: Now that Medium and others can’t rely on Google for traffic, they’re building private platforms for writing, with AI and social at the center.
articles.body: For the first time ever, Medium is becoming more than just a blogging platform. The company is launching a new app, called TK, that combines note taking and journaling with something resembling a private social network. The app is meant to get you writing more, and help you share that writing with friends and fans. And it’s part of a much bigger idea about blogging, and a much broader thesis about the state of the internet. “I don’t think we’ve actually had a launch of anything important since 2017,” Medium CEO Tony Stubblebine tells me over Zoom, a few days ahead of the company’s biggest launch in apparently almost a decade. That was when Medium’s then-CEO, Ev Williams, decided to quit chasing ad dollars and become a subscription business. “It’s clear that the broken system is ad-driven media on the internet,” Williams wrote at the time. “It simply doesn’t serve people. In fact, it’s not designed to.” Medium began charging for access to most content. “We got out of the attention economy,” Stubblebine says now. The trend Williams saw back then, though, has only accelerated and metastasized. AI companies are hoovering up any content they can get their hands on, legality be damned; search engines and chatbots are sending less and less traffic back to the web. Medium, like most websites on the internet, relies on Google for a huge portion of its traffic — in the time of Google Zero, that’s an existential risk. “When Google started taking away all the traffic,” Stubblebine says, “what I told them is that this hurts us, but it also hurts you, because I’ll just tell you what my product roadmap is going to do: I’m going to switch to private blogging… We’re just going to take everything underground.” [Image: TK is for writing — but it’s also for taking quick notes and finding them later. All of which brings us back to TK, an app and network that has no use or need for Google referrals. The idea behind TK is fairly straightforward: It’s a barebones note-taking app, with emphasis on daily journal-style notes and longer-form writing. The app itself is nice enough, like an ultra-minimalist take on Evernote, but it’s the stuff around the writing that has Stubblebine most excited. For one thing, you can point an AI model at your writing, and use it to help organize or make sense of all the notes you’ve been taking, by searching through your notes or asking for feedback on your writing. “TK” is both the name of the app and a shortcut in it: type the letters (which writers use frequently as a placeholder — they’re easy to find later, since the letters T and K hardly ever appear next to each other otherwise) and you can summon the model to fill in a bit of information for you. Stubblebine refers to “Unix pipes” a few times in our conversation, and his idea is to use the large language models to do some of the grunt work of both creating and managing notes. [Image: Libraries — private blogs — are the core social concept of TK. Once you’ve written something – and Stubblebine emphasizes that it doesn’t have to be a blog post — you can then share it however you like. You can share it via links or email the way you’d share a Google Doc, and collaborators can write, comment, and leave emoji reactions. You can also add your writing to what TK calls Libraries. Stubblebine calls the Libraries concept “private blogging,” which is a good metaphor. The early Libraries I’ve seen in the app are mostly centered around a topic, and people can contribute their writing on that topic. There’s no public face to any of it; it’s just a blog for and by its authors. Sometimes a few of them, sometimes a few hundred. There are groups sharing their ongoing book projects, swapping recipes, and posting poetry drafts, all for the eyes of only the other people in the group. It’s blogging meets group chats. This concept of private blogging is a big part of the future of Medium. “Medium is, at some level, performative,” Stubblebine says. “You have to want to share yourself with the world.” But in a post-Google world, he says, that’s essentially impossible. TK doesn’t measure pageviews or reward authors for getting traffic. “This is a community that’s going to give you feedback and encouragement,” Stubblebine says. “It’s not about the drive to be noticed.” Features like this, he says, are coming to the broader Medium platform soon. TK is now available, for free, via apps for the web, Android, and iOS. (Stubblebine says a native desktop app is also coming soon.) If TK works, though, it could be a crucial new way for Medium to make money. Obviously, Stubblebine says, there are ways to make money from private and paywalled content. That’s the newsletter business. But also, he wonders, what if there’s a way to package up all the best stuff from the Recipe Box library and charge people, or AI agents, for access? “The generic web is getting dumber and dumber,” Stubblebine says. If AI is the future, “it needs to be based on this layer of human intelligence.” And all that intelligence might be better off outside the confines of the Google algorithm.

articles.title: White House staff treated Trump like a ‘baby’: Calley Means
articles.summary: Calley Means, former aide to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., on Sunday said in an interview that White House staffers treated President Trump like a “baby.” Means, who resigned from his position last month, said on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” that the president “has been subverted” by top aides…
articles.body:
Calley Means, former aide to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., on Sunday said in an interview that White House staffers treated President Trump like a “baby.”

Means, who resigned from his position last month, said on CBS News’s “ Face the Nation ” that the president “has been subverted” by top aides and strategists. Means had claimed on “ The Joe Rogan Experience ” that White House staffers were also hindering Kennedy’s MAHA agenda by blocking popular policy items.

“I think [Trump] had severe poor advice from people, I think, who treated him like a baby in many respects and used him,” Means told “Face the Nation” host Margaret Brennan, who pressed him on this point.

Means added that these staffers “would block access to” information from Trump “all the time.”

“I would be not surprised at all, you know, if they had very short conversations on these issues, you know, where the president is extremely busy and the president said, ‘OK, whatever,’ and then they use ––” he said, before Brennan interjected, “Or he’s not interested.”

“Yes, then they used that,” Means replied. “Like it’s all –– it is all like the president wants this.”

The topic emerged after Brennan, at the start of the interview, noted Means’s recent remarks about the administration blocking health policies “that you were trying to get passed.” Means said this was specifically about allies of former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles “relentlessly pushing HHS to find a pathway for” fruit-flavored electronic cigarettes.

“They would flag something –– ‘Oh this is an important issue,'” he said. “[Trump] would say something and then they would jam it down saying it’s a president’s priority for their priorities. I don’t think President Trump ran, you know, as a primary purpose to help these industries.”

He later said Trump “has a generational coalition with” Kennedy and “wants to go hard on the issue of improving health for children.”

Means, in his interview on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” had accused Wiles of having a “stranglehold” on policy decisions, and he said she blocked an HHS food initiative out of fear it would hurt political donations from the sugar industry.

Trump political adviser James Blair told The Washington Post in a statement that Means’s claims and the “implication of corruption towards me and all the others referenced by Calley is scurrilous, false and defamatory.”

“I couldn’t tell you who donors are to what organizations other than minimal passing knowledge, because I am not a fundraiser and have no role in fundraising,” he told the outlet.

Brennan asked Means on Sunday if it was his “intention” to have Wiles removed from her post before he left the administration.

Means concurred, having cheered Stephen Miller as Wiles’s replacement and saying that the new chief of staff “wants to get transformative things done” with Kennedy and Trump “that are not partisan but structural.” He noted Miller could work with other health-focused Democrats such as Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.).

articles.title: Nvidia stock slides after company launches probe into Huang
articles.summary: Shares of Nvidia fell Monday morning, after the company opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. articles.body:
Shares of Nvidia fell Monday morning, after the company opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy.

The company’s stock opened down 7.3 percent from Friday’s closing bell, and it ticked down to $170.24 per share during early-morning trading. That marked the lowest point for the chipmaker’s stock since late March.

As recently as last Wednesday, investors were trading Nvidia’s stock at greater than $200 per share. The company’s stock hit an all-time high in early October, reaching $243.37 per share.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday it was opening an “independent investigation” regarding “recent reporting” of Huang being the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

The New York Times reported on Oct. 29 that Huang had a “close relationship” with Alice Huang — the two are not related — last year, while the latter illegally smuggled advanced AI chips into China.

Jensen Huang, after his company initially dismissed the report , admitted to the affair in a company memo, Bloomberg reported Sunday. The Nvidia CEO reportedly said he was “unfaithful” to his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang, and his actions “hurt her and our children.”

Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday a committee of “independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel” will lead the investigation into Jensen Huang. The Taiwanese American executive has led Nvidia since he founded the firm in 1993.

“The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the board said.

“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” the board added, noting Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.”

GOP Reps. John Moolenaar (Mich.), Brian Mast (Fla.) and Rick Crawford (Ark.) last week asked Huang to join lawmakers for a closed-door briefing regarding the matter on Nov. 18.

The three lawmakers respectively chair the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.

President Trump defended Huang on Sunday, calling the Nvidia CEO a “fine person” who has “done such an incredible job.”

Trump told reporters, “I think he probably has an excuse for it,” adding Huang should remain Nvidia’s CEO.

articles.title: Who is Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO facing probe over affair with alleged spy

Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday it is opening a probe into reports that Huang had been “the…
articles.body:
Jensen Huang, longtime CEO of the AI chip giant Nvidia, is facing an investigation from the company’s board after disclosing he had a romantic relationship with a woman that U.S. officials have accused of spying for China.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday it is opening a probe into reports that Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Huang, who helped found Nvidia in the 1990s, has overseen the firm’s meteoric rise from a relatively obscure chipmaker for video games to one of the biggest companies in the world.

Nvidia’s chips are highly sought after in the tech world, powering the breakneck development of AI. With this level of demand, the company rapidly grew from a market capitalization of less than $1 trillion in early 2023 to the first to cross $5 trillion in late 2025.

As the chipmaker emerged as a major player in the AI space, Huang has become a key ally to President Trump, frequently making visits to Washington.

He joined the president at a Chinese state dinner in September, where he sat at the same table as Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. In October, Huang also received the National Medal of Science from Trump, alongside several other tech executives.

The Nvidia chief has advocated for fewer restrictions on chips sales to China, arguing it is crucial to keep Beijing dependent on American-made infrastructure.

But his close ties to the president became a source of concern after U.S. officials found that Huang had a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed who they concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset, The New York Times reported late last month.

While Nvidia initially dismissed the allegations, its CEO appeared to acknowledge his relationship with the Megaspeed executive in a recent message to employees.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Nvidia’s Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” he added of the board’s probe. “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.”

The investigation, which is being overseen by a committee of independent directors, will prioritize U.S. national and economic security, although the board said it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”

The company’s stock took a hit Monday morning, opening down 7.3 percent from Friday’s closing bell. It marked the lowest point for the chipmaker’s shares since late March.

“Today’s news will not slow NVIDIA,” a company spokesperson said in a statement. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.”

articles.title: Biden scaling back book tour after cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: Former President Biden on Sunday said he was scaling back the book tour for his upcoming presidential memoir due to his ongoing cancer diagnosis. “While writing the book, I was diagnosed with cancer, a disease known all too well to millions of Americans and their families,” the former president said in a statement about the…
articles.body:
Former President Biden on Sunday said he was scaling back the book tour for his upcoming presidential memoir due to his ongoing cancer diagnosis.

“While writing the book, I was diagnosed with cancer, a disease known all too well to millions of Americans and their families,” the former president said in a statement about the process of writing “Promise Me, America,” out Nov. 17.

“My doctors continue to be encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment,” he added.

Biden said the “prayers and kind words and well wishes from so many of you have meant more to” him and former first lady Jill Biden” and our family than you can ever know.”

“Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me,” he continued. “But sometimes it slows me down. What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves.”

The former president’s office revealed in May 2025 , four months after he left office, that he was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer with bone metastasis, though doctors said his cancer was “hormone sensitive.” He completed his treatment in October 2025.

Biden said in September that his radiation treatment “ worked as intended ” and continued to work on his memoir.

His son Hunter Biden told BBC’s “Newsnight” in August that his father’s cancer had spread to other parts of his body, calling it “very debilitating” and that watching the former president’s health decline has been “really hard.”

“The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good,” the younger Biden said at the time.

Jill Biden called her husband’s diagnosis “shocking” and said White House physicians “somehow” missed detecting his cancer.

The memoir will cover the former president’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic and his decision to run for a second term. The book also “reveals the deeply agonizing calculation behind his decision in the summer of 2024 to step aside from the presidential race and to put his party and the nation before his personal ambitions,” according to the publisher Hachette Book Group .

His office also stated last year that he had undergone Mohs surgery to cut away thin layers of skin to be examined for signs of cancer, until no signs are found.
