articles.title: Conservation Fund buys Jimmy Carter family farm in Georgia
articles.summary: Former President Jimmy Carter’s family farm in Georgia has been sold to a conservation group for $8.5 million, with plans to preserve the land and eventually open it to the public. The Conservation Fund announced Monday that it had acquired the roughly 2,458-acre land outside Plains, Ga., where the nation’s 39th president grew up and…
articles.body:
Former President Jimmy Carter’s family farm in Georgia has been sold to a conservation group for $8.5 million, with plans to preserve the land and eventually open it to the public.

The Conservation Fund announced Monday that it had acquired the roughly 2,458-acre land outside Plains, Ga., where the nation’s 39th president grew up and continued to return to throughout his life.

“We’re honored to help ensure this land remains [a] healthy habitat for wildlife, and we look forward to the day it is open to everyone who wants to experience it,” Stacy Funderburke, the organization’s vice president for the central Southeast region, said in a statement to WTVM.

In a separate statement to the outlet, Carter’s grandson expressed his gratitude for the acquisition.

“For our family, this land was always about more than a farm. It was home — a place my grandparents treasured. We’re grateful to The Conservation Fund and to everyone working to make sure it’s protected for generations to come,” said Jason Carter.

The nonprofit plans to transfer the property to the Georgia Department of Natural Resources in 2028, expanding the nearby Lanahassee Creek Wildlife Management Area to nearly 7,000 acres. The land could open to the public for hunting, fishing and other outdoor activities as early as 2027.

“Long before Jimmy Carter protected millions of acres across America, he was a boy working the fields and roaming the woods of southwest Georgia,” said Funderburke. “This land has shaped him and his legacy, and he never stopped coming home to it.”

Carter, who died in December 2024 at age 100, spent much of his childhood working alongside his father on the family farm, growing peanuts and other crops. He returned to Plains in 1952 after leaving the Navy following his father’s death to take over the family business.

The acquisition also preserves a piece of Carter’s environmental legacy. During his presidency, he signed the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act of 1980, which protected more than 104 million acres in what remains the largest expansion of protected public lands in U.S. history.

articles.title: Hegseth plans press conference, says he’s ‘not worried’ about impeachment push
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said he plans to hold a press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday morning and argued that he is “not worried” about the impeachment articles Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) plans to reintroduce against him this week. “We’re not worried about that,” Hegseth told reporters in Newport, R.I., on Monday when asked…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said he plans to hold a press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday morning and argued that he is “not worried” about the impeachment articles Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) plans to reintroduce against him this week.

“We’re not worried about that,” Hegseth told reporters in Newport, R.I., on Monday when asked about Massie’s impeachment salvo, which he first introduced in September.

“I’ll tell you this. Actually, I hope all of you will join us. We’re going to do a press conference tomorrow morning at the Pentagon on that very topic,” the Pentagon chief added. “So I’ll save my remarks there.”

The Pentagon confirmed the press conference will start at 8 a.m. ET, the first one Hegseth has held in over six months. The last press conference at the Pentagon took place on May 5.

The press conference comes as Massie’s impeachment push is gaining steam on Capitol Hill with even some House Republicans weighing whether to support the resolution following the Democratic Party’s dominant showing during the midterm elections.

Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), the chair of the powerful House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, said Friday on The Hill’s sister network NewsNation that “there’s a lot of questions” in the Republican conference about Hegseth.

“But I can tell you with a high level of confidence that … there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth. We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran,” Comer said. “No one’s happy about Iran, and I think the Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is likely to become the House Speaker come January, said on Sunday that he is a “hard yes” when it comes to impeaching Hegseth.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran,” Jeffries said ABC News’s “This Week.”

President Trump has stood publicly behind Hegseth, but the commander-in-chief has asked advisers and allies about the defense secretary’s standing, The Hill previously reported .

Hegseth lambasted the articles of impeachment on Thursday as being authored by a “disgruntled, defeated congressman.”

“Just like they tried against President Trump twice. You see, their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that,” the Pentagon chief said on Thursday.

Massie will hold a press conference himself at 3:30 p.m. ET on Monday to discuss his articles of impeachment.

articles.title: DeSantis rips ‘short-sighted’ College Football Playoff expansion
articles.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) is not a fan of an expanded college football playoff. In a social media post on Monday, the Florida governor called the move “short-sighted,” saying it “might bolster profits in the near term but will further erode what has traditionally made college football special.” ESPN and the College Football Playoff…
articles.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) is not a fan of an expanded college football playoff.

In a social media post on Monday, the Florida governor called the move “short-sighted,” saying it “might bolster profits in the near term but will further erode what has traditionally made college football special.”

ESPN and the College Football Playoff Committee announced earlier in the day that the single elimination postseason tournament would be expanded from 12 to 24 teams beginning with the conclusion of the 2027 season.

With the expansion came an extension of playoff media rights deal with ESPN, totaling more than $1 billion and running through the next five seasons.

DeSantis’s comment comes as lawmakers on Capitol Hill have debated for months major legislation regulating the big business of college sports around issues like the transfer portal; name, image and likeness compensation and media rights.

The “Protect College Sports” Act, a bill passed by the Senate this fall, appears unlikely to pass before the end of the year, with most observers predicting that Democrats winning control of the House and Senate could push the legislation to the backburner.

President Trump has insisted on Congress passing meaningful legislation to address major issues around college sports, and many in his party have bemoaned a growing arms race at top schools fueled in part by prime time postseason match-ups for live television audiences.

The NCAA, which does not operate the College Football Playoff, earlier this year announced it was expanding its annual men’s and women’s basketball tournaments, from 68 to 76 teams.

DeSantis, seen as a possible GOP candidate for president in 2028 , last week called Republican losses in the midterm elections an “extinction level” event for the party.

articles.title: France blames Iran for mass-hacks targeting freezers in grocery stores and blood banks | TechCrunch
articles.summary: France's foreign minister blamed Iran for launching at least two waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigerated and freezer units across France and wider Europe.
articles.body:
The French government has formally blamed Iran for launching cyberattacks that targeted thousands of internet-connected industrial refrigerated and freezer units across the country and broader Europe.

This is the latest in a string of destructive cyberattacks attributed to Iran this year, following a spate of hacks targeting U.S. water providers and other online intrusions that caused mass-disruption to U.S. medical device maker Stryker and others.

The U.S. government linked the attacks to pro-Iranian hacktivists who are working for Tehran, likely in response to the U.S./Israel-led war against Iran which killed its supreme leader in February.

Two recent waves of cyberattacks throughout October and into November saw hackers remotely break into web-based controllers that manage fleets of industrial cold and chilling units at grocery stores and retail supermarkets, and raise the temperatures to spoil food and destroy goods. Medical blood banks were also hacked but the attacks were stopped before any blood was spoiled, according to the French Blood Establishment .

Security researchers have since warned that the web-based controllers are vulnerable to remote hacks, with some of the affected models made by Danish company Danfoss no longer receiving security fixes.

In a statement given to reporters in Paris on Monday, French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said: “I am able to confirm that responsibility for this act lies with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” referring to Iran’s military and hackers.

“This was an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression; it represents the first large-scale act of sabotage on our national territory and constitutes a major assault on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people,” said Barrot, adding that the hacks will “not go without consequences.”

The French government has summoned Iran’s ambassador. Reuters first reported France’s attribution to Iran, citing sources ahead of the foreign minister’s remarks. The French government said it would also issue European-wide sanctions against those who carried out the hacks. Barrot said that the matter was now in the hands of the French justice system.

A spokesperson for Iran’s consulate in New York did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The U.S. government is also reportedly looking into whether freezer units on military bases were hacked, following reports of similar outages and disruption earlier this year. U.S. officials have reportedly also linked the freezer-related cyberattack to Iran, but the intelligence community has not yet made a formal or public attribution.

articles.title: New AI malware ranks victims by how much they're worth
articles.summary: VOLTA-AUTODOXER malware uses AI to analyze stolen data and rank victims by potential value, helping criminals target the most profitable accounts.
articles.body: You probably know that hackers want your passwords, credit card information and other personal details. But what if they could also figure out how much you're worth to them? That's exactly what researchers say a newly discovered malware strain is designed to do. It steals information from your computer, studies your digital life and then uses artificial intelligence to build a detailed profile of you. The goal? Help criminals decide which victims deserve more attention and which stolen accounts could bring in the most money. The malware is called VOLTA-AUTODOXER, and researchers at Cisco Talos uncovered it through a cybersecurity research project focused on AI-powered threats. What caught my attention is how it can take everyday details about your life and turn them into something criminals could use against you. Even a food delivery receipt could help reveal where you live. Here's how this malware works, what it could reveal about you and the steps you can take to protect yourself. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. WINDOWS MALWARE USES GROK AI TO HELP STAY HIDDEN, RESEARCHERS SAY How this new AI malware works Most information-stealing malware follows a familiar pattern. It gets onto your computer, collects whatever sensitive information it can find and sends that data back to criminals. VOLTA-AUTODOXER takes that process further by using AI to evaluate the information after collecting it. According to Cisco Talos, the Windows malware can steal saved browser passwords, payment card information and login sessions. It also targets cryptocurrency wallets and certain work-related credentials. Once it collects that information, it builds a detailed report about the person using the computer. That report can include your location, employer and clues about your age. The malware can also collect saved Wi-Fi passwords, screenshots and information from applications such as Microsoft Outlook and Slack. Researchers even found that it attempts to crack cryptocurrency wallet vaults. Then comes the AI component. The malware sends the information to an AI model through a platform called OpenRouter. The model receives instructions to act like an intelligence analyst and determine which stolen information could be the most valuable. Think about that for a moment. Instead of a criminal manually reviewing hundreds of stolen accounts, AI can help sort through the information and identify potentially profitable targets. And the AI analysis is optional. Even if that part fails or cannot run, the malware can still collect information and send it to the attacker. Your food delivery history could reveal more than you think Here's where this gets especially personal. VOLTA-AUTODOXER can search for clues about your home address, employer and financial information. Researchers found that it can also use stolen account access to examine Gmail receipts and food delivery orders. For example, the malware looks for purchase information from services such as Uber Eats and DoorDash. It can also examine receipts from Amazon and other retailers. Those records may help confirm where you live. And it goes further. Using stolen login sessions, the malware can retrieve order histories directly from Uber Eats and DoorDash. It can also search Gmail for receipts from Grubhub, Walmart and PayPal. That gives criminals another way to connect your online activity to your actual identity. The information goes well beyond your address. The malware can collect clues about your age, workplace and online accounts. It can even look at Roblox accounts to estimate the value of virtual items. Individually, some of these details might seem harmless. But when AI combines them, criminals could develop a much clearer understanding of your personal and financial life. AI decides which stolen information could be worth money The most concerning part of VOLTA-AUTODOXER comes after the information has been collected. The malware asks AI to create a report that ranks the victim's assets according to their potential value. Researchers found that the instructions include a section called "WHAT THEY'RE WORTH." The AI is asked to identify valuable information and assign low, medium or high rankings. Another section called "THEIR OPSEC" examines the victim's security habits, including password practices. In other words, the malware is designed to help criminals understand what they might gain and how well someone has protected their accounts. Cisco Talos found that the malware uses Anthropic's Claude as its default AI model. If the model refuses the request, the malware can try Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash. That fallback system is especially revealing. Whoever developed the malware anticipated that an AI model might refuse to help and built a way to try another model. The malware can also send the resulting assessment to criminals through Telegram. That means an attacker could potentially receive an organized report without having to study all the stolen information personally. There's an important point here. Researchers identified these capabilities by analyzing the malware's code. They have not established that criminals have successfully used these AI-generated rankings to select real-world victims for additional attacks. AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS The malware can delete itself after stealing your data Another concerning capability is VOLTA-AUTODOXER's ability to remove its main executable after completing its work. That could make an infection harder to investigate. However, Cisco Talos found that the malware may leave behind a diagnostic file called volta_debug.txt. That file can contain a record of what the malware collected and whether the AI analysis succeeded. For security investigators, it could provide valuable clues about what happened. There's another detail worth knowing. The malware uses the infected computer's own internet connection to contact the AI service. Researchers also found that its observed network destinations belong to third-party services rather than infrastructure owned by the attacker. That could make suspicious activity less obvious, although it does not guarantee the malware will escape detection. Researchers also found evidence suggesting the malware was designed as a customizable product. Its developer appears to have created a system where different criminals could supply their own settings and receive a customized version. Cisco Talos believes this could make AI-powered victim profiling available to criminals who lack advanced technical skills. However, researchers have not confirmed that the malware is being sold. What researchers still don't know There are some important unanswered questions. Cisco Talos first observed the analyzed sample on October 11, 2026, but researchers have not established how many computers VOLTA-AUTODOXER has infected or how widely it has spread. They also have not confirmed a specific campaign distributing this malware. That means there's no evidence in the published findings that this malware is currently infecting large numbers of everyday computer users. Still, its capabilities show how criminals could use AI to get more value from information they already know how to steal. And for now, there's no confirmed method of distribution for VOLTA-AUTODOXER. That's why it's important to focus on protecting your computer against information-stealing malware in general rather than assuming this particular threat arrives through a specific type of message or download. How to protect yourself from AI-powered malware You don't need to understand how AI works to reduce your risk. VOLTA-AUTODOXER still needs access to your computer before it can collect sensitive information. That means many of the same precautions that protect against traditional malware can help here, too. Here are some practical steps worth taking. 1. Use strong antivirus protection One of the best ways to protect yourself is to have strong antivirus software running on your devices. Good security software can help detect malicious downloads, suspicious programs and other threats before they steal your information. Keep your protection updated and run regular scans. Look for software that monitors suspicious behavior in addition to scanning for known threats. That's especially helpful when dealing with malware designed to hide its activity or delete itself after an attack. Protect passwords saved on your computer VOLTA-AUTODOXER specifically targets credentials stored in web browsers. Consider using a reputable password manager that protects your passwords in an encrypted vault instead. Create a strong, unique password for every important account. That way, one stolen password won't automatically give criminals access to other services. However, a password manager alone cannot guarantee protection if your computer has already been compromised. Some malware can steal active login sessions or capture sensitive information while you're using it. 3. Turn on two-factor authentication Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for your email, financial accounts and other important services. Whenever possible, use passkeys or a hardware security key. However, remember that some information-stealing malware can steal active login sessions. That means 2FA alone may not stop every account takeover. If you suspect an infection, sign out of existing sessions after securing your device. 4. Keep Windows and your applications updated Install Windows security updates and keep your browser current. Updates can close vulnerabilities that attackers exploit to install malware. Also, avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites. Be especially cautious about unexpected attachments or messages urging you to install something immediately. And never copy commands into Windows PowerShell, Command Prompt or the Run dialog because a random website tells you to fix a problem. Criminals have used these tactics to trick people into installing other information-stealing malware. HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS 5. Reduce the personal information criminals can find VOLTA-AUTODOXER shows how seemingly unrelated personal details can help criminals build a profile of you. However, they can help reduce the amount of personal information available through public data broker listings. Watch for signs of identity theft Because this malware collects financial and identifying information, consider using an identity theft protection service. Such services can monitor for certain signs of misuse and alert you to suspicious activity. You should also review your financial statements and credit reports regularly. If criminals gain access to your information, early detection could help limit the damage. You can also place a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. That includes certain Microsoft account tokens, cloud credentials and Slack workspace details. If you use your computer for work, avoid storing sensitive access keys in unprotected files. Follow your company's security policies and report suspicious activity to your IT department immediately. Cisco Talos also identified a technique that attempts to bypass Chrome's App-Bound Encryption protection. Organizations can reduce that risk by controlling which programs can launch Chrome in headless mode. That is a more technical safeguard your IT or security team can evaluate. What to do if you think your computer has been infected If you suspect malware has stolen your information, act quickly. Most importantly, don't assume you're safe because the suspicious program has disappeared. This malware can delete itself after stealing your information, and the stolen credentials may still be usable by criminals. Kurt's key takeaways What concerns me most about VOLTA-AUTODOXER is how much someone could learn about you just by getting into your computer. Think about what's sitting on your device right now. Maybe you've saved a few passwords in your browser. Your email probably contains years of receipts, including orders delivered right to your front door. Now, consider what happens when a criminal feeds all that information into AI and asks one simple question: How much is this person worth? That's what caught my attention about this research. The malware is designed to do the homework for the criminal and help identify which stolen information deserves the most attention. We still don't know how widely VOLTA-AUTODOXER has spread, so there's no reason to assume your computer has been targeted. But I do think this gives us a pretty good idea of where cybercrime could be heading. The less work criminals have to do themselves, the easier it could become for them to target more people. And that's one more reason to take your personal information seriously before someone gets hold of it. How would you feel knowing that hackers could use AI to put a dollar value on your personal information? And do you think AI companies should do more to prevent criminals from using their technology this way? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Bacon ‘torn’ over whether to back Hegseth impeachment
articles.summary: Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), a centrist Republican retiring from the Congress who has criticized President Trump on foreign policy and other matters, on Monday said he is conflicted about the effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth being led by a fellow GOP lawmaker. “The areas that concern me the most about the secretary aren’t…
articles.body:
Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), a centrist Republican retiring from the Congress who has criticized President Trump on foreign policy and other matters, on Monday said he is conflicted about the effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth being led by a fellow GOP lawmaker.

“The areas that concern me the most about the secretary aren’t in the articles of impeachment,” Bacon told CNN’s Manu Raju in a video posted to the social platform X, referencing an effort from Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) for impeachment.

“The firing and redlining of 80 generals and flag — or admirals, the — withholding appropriated money all year for Ukraine,” he added.

“I’m not the only one that feels that way, there’s a bunch of us that have been talking about it,” Bacon added. “So, this is, you know, Congressman Massie’s impeachment, he’s got more of a libertarian spirit to his write–up. And I think some of us don’t feel comfortable with his justifications, but I think there’s other ones out there. So, that’s what I’m grappling with.”

Bacon, in response to a direct question, said he was torn on the issue.

He said he would “be more inclined to” back articles of impeachment that touched more directly on his own reasons for feeling uneasy about Hegseth, and that he would also support Hegseth’s resignation.

On Monday, Massie followed through on a promise to bring articles of impeachment targeting Hegseth. The Kentucky Republican read the articles out loud on the House floor a little after 2 p.m.

Earlier Monday, Hegseth said he wasn’t “worried “ about Massie’s effort and said he would have a press conference the following morning on the matter.

The impeachment effort comes after Republicans suffered massive defeats in last week’s midterm elections.

Over the weekend , President Trump expressed concerns over some Democrats pushing for the impeachment of Republican officials. The president called the threats “extortion at the highest level” and requested the Justice Department “look into this.”

“The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people … with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so, and there have been no impeachable acts committed, or even thought of, by the victims of this illegal process,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post Saturday.

The Hill has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

articles.title: Supreme Court allows Big Bend border construction to continue in Texas, siding with Trump
articles.summary: The Supreme Court is allowing border barrier construction to continue in and around Big Bend National Park in Texas, in a win for the Trump administration. The justices on Monday halted a lower court’s decision last month to pause the construction while the underlying case against it plays out. In a brief statement outlining its…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court is allowing border barrier construction to continue in and around Big Bend National Park in Texas, in a win for the Trump administration.

The justices on Monday halted a lower court’s decision last month to pause the construction while the underlying case against it plays out.

In a brief statement outlining its decision, the high court said that the lower one’s injunction “impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.”

The statement did not explicitly state which justices supported the decision, though it said that Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson disagreed with it and would have denied the government’s request to halt the lower court ruling.

Earlier this year, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem waived environmental laws to expedite the construction of barriers and roads in the Big Bend area.

The move has been controversial, as bipartisan locals have said that the construction could harm the local economy and environment and hamper their ability to recreate in the area.

The administration has said it will not build a large border wall inside the national park but is pursuing other construction activity there.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth faces House impeachment vote amid controversy over Iran War
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on Monday escalated his effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, forcing a House vote later in the week to remove a Defense secretary who’s emerged as among the most controversial figures of President Trump’s second term. The development marks the second time in two months that Massie has sought to oust the…
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on Monday escalated his effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, forcing a House vote later in the week to remove a Defense secretary who’s emerged as among the most controversial figures of President Trump’s second term.

The development marks the second time in two months that Massie has sought to oust the Pentagon chief. On the first occasion, House GOP leaders blocked the effort by sending lawmakers home a day early for the pre-midterm recess, effectively avoiding a vote that might have been difficult for some vulnerable incumbents.

But that tactic merely delayed the inevitable. And Massie wasted no time revisiting the issue in the lame duck, stepping to the House floor on Congress’s first day back to Washington to reintroduce his resolution.

“Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation, notwithstanding the absence of congressional authorization, an attack upon the United States giving rise to the national emergency contemplated by law, or an imminent threat requiring immediate defensive action, thereby substituting unlawful executive action for the constitutional and statutory judgment of Congress,” Massie said Monday on the House floor.

“In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense and subversive of constitutional government, to the great prejudice of the cause of law and justice, and to the manifest injury of the people of the United States of America,” the Kentucky Republican said.

It’s unclear if the measure has the support to pass while Republicans still control the lower chamber. Despite some GOP criticism of the Pentagon chief, Massie has been the lonely Republican calling for Hegseth to be removed from office.

But the midterm rout suffered by the Republicans could be a factor in the vote, as dozens of GOP incumbents who lost their reelection bids will be newly liberated to vote their consciences — and their legacies — without fear of political repercussions from Trump or the MAGA faithful who still support him.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), a frequent Hegseth critic who was on the fence on impeachment before the elections, was sounding a different tune on Monday, suggesting he is ready to back Massie’s resolution.

Even Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), a Trump ally who chairs the powerful House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, said voters have soured on Hegseth, particularly over his handling of the Iran War, and suggested that Republicans in the Capitol are doing the same.

“I can tell you with a high level of confidence that … there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth,” Comer told NewsNation on Friday . “We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran, and I think the Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.”

Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.), the chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, did not rule out impeaching Hegseth and voiced dissatisfaction about the U.S. handling of the Iran war.

“I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment,” Hill said during his Sunday appearance on CBS’s “Face the Nation.”

Other Republicans, however, are lining up behind Hegseth, praising the Defense chief for what they see as bringing a warrior ethic back to the Pentagon.

Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wisc.), a Hegseth ally who sits on the House Armed Services Committee (HASC) called Massie “self-aggrandizing twit who never served in the military” and his impeachment effort “pathetic.”

Van Orden wrote Monday that Hegseth’s leadership of the Pentagon has led to the “highest morale in decades, the prosecution of some of the most extraordinary combat ops in the history of warfare and record recruiting .”

Hegseth previously boosted Van Orden in his reelection bid against Democrat Rebecca Cooke during a trip to Eau Claire, Wisc. Van Orden lost the race last week.

And the administration is standing behind the defense secretary with Secretary of State Marco Rubio praising him for doing a “great job.”

“I’ve worked with him every single day on many of these topics. I’ve seen the work he does and the professionalism he brings to it. He’s very smart. He works very hard,” Rubio, who also serves as Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters on Monday. “He puts a lot of hours into this, and on all the policy issues we’ve worked on together, I think he’s done a very good job.”

Democrats, meanwhile, are expected to support Hegseth’s ouster en masse, especially after House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who had declined to endorse Massie’s resolution before the midterms, quickly changed course and threw his full weight behind the measure .

Massie’s eight impeachment articles accuse the Pentagon chief of abusing his powers in relation to several Pentagon operations, including Hegseth’s handling of the Iran War and the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in international waters.

Jeffries’s full-throated support gives the resolution a big boost. Before the elections, Jeffries had kept his powder dry on the issue , perhaps out of caution not to add fuel to Trump’s warnings that Democrats, if given control of the House, would prioritize impeachments above everything else to settle old political scores.

articles.title: Hegseth orders major revamp of military education
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday ordered sweeping changes to the U.S. military’s professional education system, prioritizing skills that will win wars — an overhaul that comes as the Pentagon chief faces mounting calls for his impeachment. “When a commandant approves a curriculum, the essential question before them is not, ‘Is this intellectually fashionable?’ .…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday ordered sweeping changes to the U.S. military’s professional education system, prioritizing skills that will win wars — an overhaul that comes as the Pentagon chief faces mounting calls for his impeachment .

“When a commandant approves a curriculum, the essential question before them is not, ‘Is this intellectually fashionable?’ . . . The only question that matters to the American republic is this: Will it help us achieve victory?” Hegseth said in a speech at the Naval War College.

A memo signed by Hegseth released the same day lays out 33 reforms and directives across the military’s Senior Service Colleges and Intermediate Level Education institutions, to be “effective immediately.”

He argues that professional military education (PME) “has stagnated” and drifted from its core purpose of preparing officers to fight and win wars, trading “combat readiness for theory” and indulging “ideological distractions over practical warfighting.”

“The fundamental purpose of the Armed Forces of the United States is to fight and win our Nation’s wars. There is no substitute for victory,” Hegseth writes.

“We will evaluate our educational institutions by a singular standard: ‘Does this program forge leaders who will win America’s wars?’” he later adds. “If an activity, course, or policy does not contribute directly to lethality, readiness, and strategic victory, it has no place in this Department.”

The memo is another step in Hegseth’s push to overhaul the military’s higher education, an effort that has seen the freezing of appointments of civilian staff to tenured positions at U.S. military service academies; the cancellation of members of the military attending some of the country’s top-ranked colleges and universities; and the banning of hundreds of library books at the Naval Academy.

War colleges are separate from the service academies and offer professional military education to Pentagon civilians, high-ranking officers and international partners, focusing on national security, joint operations and strategy.

Hegseth’s effort comes as Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) plans to reintroduce the impeachment articles against him Monday afternoon over his role in the ongoing and deeply unpopular Iran war.

The impeachment push has been gaining steam on Capitol Hill since Massie first introduced the idea in September, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) — likely to become the House Speaker come January — on Sunday saying that he is a “hard yes” when it comes to impeaching the Pentagon chief.

President Trump has publicly stood behind Hegseth, but the commander-in-chief as of late has been asking advisers and allies about his defense secretary’s standing, The Hill previously reported .

Hegseth has remained defiant, posting a video to social media last week that describes Massie’s articles as “sham articles of impeachment” authored by a “disgruntled, defeated congressman.”

In his push to change PME, Hegseth directs institutions to refocus their mission statements “toward achieving decisive military victory in combat,” and orders mandatory, end-of-course wargames or comprehensive exams “to test student mastery of core national security and joint warfighting material,” an event that he says should be heavily weighted toward the student’s final grade.

In addition, he orders the realignment of the civilian-faculty ratio at schools “to ensure that the majority of full-time faculty possess direct military experience and defense experience.” Newly arrived civilian faculty members will be put under three-year, performance-based contracts evaluated on teaching effectiveness and national security research.

The memo also establishes a “warfighter chair” at all senior service colleges, to be filled with “high-performing” colonels or lieutenant colonels who have come from operational deployments in the past two years. They will be responsible for injecting real-time combat lessons into the curriculum.

Incremental adjustments will not achieve this transformation. Effective immediately, all directed reform tasks detailed in the attached implementation directive will be executed across commands and institutions,” Hegseth writes.
